1.title: Find the right sites for chargers
1.intro: Chargers earn where cars stop for a while and power is available.
pts: Types: home, workplace, destination (1-4 hours), fast (20-40 minutes).
Site scores: dwell time, traffic, nearby amenities, grid power, safety, cost to connect.
Visit three sites; count cars parked per hour.
Write a one-page site pitch to an owner.
Ask the local utility early for the power available at the site and the cost to connect.
Count cars at three times of day to see the peak and the quiet periods.
Ask the owner what they gain: footfall, rent or a share of revenue.
1.ex: Shopping centre: average stay 90 minutes, 60 EV cars a day, grid connection 150 kW available; score 4.2/5. If 25% of the cars would charge, 60 x 0.25 = 15 sessions a day is the ceiling to test. At 50 kW a 28 kWh session takes 28 / 50 = 0.56 hour, about 34 minutes, which fits inside the 90-minute stay.
1.act: Score three sites and choose one.

2.title: Know electrical and utility rules
2.intro: Charging involves electricity and public safety.
pts: Electrical work follows the provincial code and licensed electricians; permits and inspections are required.
Utility connection agreements set capacity and timing.
Accessibility and signage rules apply.
Selling electricity by the kWh is regulated by province; check how to charge.
Ask the provincial electrical authority which permit and inspection steps apply and who must hold the licence.
Ask the utility for the connection timeline and write it into your plan.
Check the provincial rule on whether you may charge by kWh, by time or by session.
2.ex: Row: 'Install a fast charger | provincial electrical authority | permit and inspection | before energising | inspection certificate'. Row: 'Charge by the kWh | provincial measurement and energy rules | check allowed method | before opening | written answer filed'. If the utility needs 12 weeks and the permit 4 weeks and they run in parallel, plan 12 weeks, not 16.
2.act: Build a rules table for one site.

3.title: Plan the installation
pts: Compute power: number of chargers x kW, with load management to share capacity.
Plan cables, trenching, lighting and drainage.
Choose connectors and payment methods that suit local cars.
Plan remote monitoring.
Have a licensed electrician size the cable and breaker; do not guess.
Lay out the bays so every cable reaches and none crosses a walkway.
Choose the load-management setting (fair share or first come) and write it down.
3.ex: 4 chargers of 50 kW on a 150 kW supply with load sharing: no more than 3 run at full power at once (3 x 50 = 150). If all 4 are in use, each gets 150 / 4 = 37.5 kW, so a 28 kWh session takes 28 / 37.5 = 0.75 hour, or 45 minutes.
3.act: Draw a site layout and load plan.

4.title: Price charging and prove the business
4.intro: Revenue per kWh, minus power cost and fees.
pts: Energy margin = selling price - energy price - network fees.
Add idle fees to free the bay.
Include maintenance, software and site lease.
Compute payback.
List the cost lines (hardware, install, connection, signs, software) and sum them.
Set the price per kWh from the margin you need, then compare with nearby prices.
Run three cases: low, medium and high sessions per day.
4.ex: Installed cost 18,000. High case: 12 sessions a day x 28 kWh x 0.18 margin = 60.48 a day, about 1,800 a month; less 400 for site, software and upkeep leaves 1,400, so payback = 18,000 / 1,400 = about 13 months. Low case: 5 sessions a day gives 25.20 a day, about 756 a month; less 400 leaves 356, so payback = 18,000 / 356 = about 51 months. Teaching figures in CAD.
4.act: Build a payback model with a low-use case.

5.title: Operate reliably
pts: Monitor remotely; alert on faults.
Respond within a set time.
Clean and inspect monthly.
Track uptime and sessions.
Write a fault response plan: who is called, in what order and within what time.
Keep spare parts for common faults (connector, cable) on a shelf.
Check payment terminals and screens weekly and record the result.
5.ex: Uptime 97% target; fault repaired within 24 hours. In a 30-day month (720 hours), 3% downtime allows only 720 x 0.03 = 21.6 hours, so one 24-hour fault alone breaks the target; spare parts on the shelf prevent this.

6.title: Win site hosts and drivers
pts: Offer revenue share to site owners.
List on charging maps.
Offer fleet plans.
Collect feedback.
Prepare a one-page revenue-share offer showing the owner's income at low, medium and high use.
List the site on charging maps and check that its details are right.
Ask five drivers what would make them return and record the answers.
6.ex: Funnel: 20 sites, 6 meetings, 2 agreements; that is 6 / 20 = 30% to a meeting and 2 / 6 = 33% to an agreement. If the owner gets 10% of a 1,800 monthly margin, the owner earns 180 and you keep 1,620.

7.title: Manage safety and grid risk
7.intro: Plan for hazards and demand peaks.
pts: Cable and trip hazards, vandalism, weather.
Peak demand charges.
Cyber security for chargers.
Insurance.
Walk the site at night and list hazards (lighting, trip points, vehicle impact) with a fix for each.
Ask the utility how demand charges are set and compute the worst month.
Change default passwords, apply updates and limit who can control the chargers.
7.ex: Risk: 'Peak demand charge | 3 x 4 | load management | ops | monthly'. Suppose the utility charged 12 per kW of monthly peak (an assumed rate; check the real tariff): a 150 kW peak costs 150 x 12 = 1,800, while limiting load to 100 kW costs 100 x 12 = 1,200, a saving of 600 a month.

8.title: Pilot and expand
pts: 90 days.
Measure sessions, kWh, uptime.
Stop rule: under 3 sessions a day after 60 days means move or adjust price.
Plan roll-out.
Set up counters for sessions, kWh, uptime and revenue before day one.
Review at day 30, 60 and 90 and adjust price or signs using the data.
Write the roll-out plan with site criteria, budget and order.
8.ex: 5.2 sessions per day; proceed. Over 90 days that is 5.2 x 90 = 468 sessions, and at 28 kWh each, 468 x 28 = 13,104 kWh. The stop rule of 3 sessions a day would be 3 x 90 = 270 sessions, so the site clears it easily.
